prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement technique that has changed what can be observed. Trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength cancels the light shift, so thousands of atoms are interrogated at once with Doppler and recoil effects removed. Systematic uncertainty and instability are now at the 1e-18 level, and the evidence is quantitative and repeated: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL operate such clocks and compare them, including across fibre links, with agreement at that level. That is the standard of experimental demonstration I trust. The consequences are concrete and still growing: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and relativistic geodesy, bounds on drifts of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, and the pending redefinition of the second. Four colleagues (Lindroth, Olsson, Danielsson, Pearce) independently rate the physics as clean and mature, and the two-name attribution (Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and first demonstration, Ye for the record accuracy, stability and many-body clock work) is the cleanest on the whole shortlist. The citation should be framed on the lattice-clock concept and its realization, not on clocks in general.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with earlier prizes. Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency comb) and Wineland and Haroche (2012, ion control, with the Al+ ion clocks) already stand in this neighbourhood, and the committee could see lattice clocks as an incremental extension of precision metrology rather than a new discovery. Katori's magic-wavelength idea also has other proposers and early developers (Lemonde, Pal'chikov, Takamoto, Ludlow) outside the credited names. And the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the application is incomplete. I would answer that the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured different enabling tools, and that a neutral-atom ensemble clock is a distinct achievement, but the committee must decide how much a metrology prize can repeat a subfield.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B012 first as a clean, original instrument, with Katori's magic-wavelength lattice and Ye's record accuracy, and notes that the redefinition of the second and the build-on from the 2005 comb prize could be argued either way.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and think her point about the redefinition is the right one to take seriously. I would not make the prize depend on it. The 1e-18 comparisons between independent labs already exist, and the Nobel criterion is the demonstrated new capability, not the SI decision. I differ slightly on the 2005 overlap: the comb is a tool that the clock uses, as a lattice clock uses lasers, and does not carry the idea. Her named omissions (Lemonde, Takamoto) are real, but the three-person limit and the supplied credit give Katori and Ye as the defensible core.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED first and trapped-ion gates second, ranks the lattice clock third, and says he defers to AMO colleagues on metrological priority and doubts that a second superconducting prize is balanced so soon after 2025.
responses.response: I accept his own caution on B005 and share the timing worry after the 2025 prize. I do not accept that circuit QED can rank above the clock on maturity right now. As a measurement matter, cQED is mostly an engineering and readout framework whose discovery claim, strong coupling in 2004, is a smaller step than the capability change the clocks gave. I do agree with his ranking of B020 above many others, which is why I keep it as my first alternative. A Cirac-Zoller-Blatt prize is credible but carries the 2012 overlap he flags, and the experimental credit (Wineland, Monroe) is not cleanly split.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because the theory prediction was followed by a clear experimental discovery and a new field, and puts the lattice clock second, citing possible overlap with earlier prizes and unsettled Katori versus Ye roles.
responses.response: His standard of prediction followed by clear clues from nature is a good one, and B042 meets it. My reservation is the one shared by Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson in their own statements: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved and twist-angle disorder limits sample reproducibility, so I am less sure that a stable physical principle has been delivered. On his clock doubt, Katori's concept and Ye's performance are separable in the record, so I do not see the roles as unsettled. I would keep B042 as my second alternative and expect it to be the stronger candidate in a few years.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B012 first, as precision atomic physics that she knows well, and notes that the clock risks being seen as an extension of the comb and ion-clock prizes. She ranks B019 Rydberg arrays last and calls it not yet a completed discovery.
responses.response: We agree on the clock, and I would add that she is better placed than I am to judge whether the credit separation from Hall and Hansch is manageable; I would like her to say explicitly whether she regards Ye's contribution as distinct from the comb work he built on. On B019 I ranked it fourth and she ranked it eighth. I now side with her more than with my own opening: recent error-correction demonstrations are impressive, but the technology is still moving, so I would not put it in a prize this year.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first and the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery second as instrument-led discoveries, and notes the problem of crediting a single name or a handful of names for a large collaboration.
responses.response: I respect the instrument-builder argument, since I also rank detector concepts highly. The attribution problem is the decisive weakness for B035 and B028. A single credited name (Halzen) cannot stand for the IceCube collaboration, and for the Higgs the three founders are leaders rather than demonstrably the originators of the decisive measurement. I ranked B028 last for exactly this reason. The clock has the opposite property: two named people each have a separable, documented contribution. I would also ask whether the neutrino sources are identified well enough; the diffuse flux is firm but most of its origin is not.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives to the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes when judging whether lattice clocks are a distinct achievement.
Whether a prize to Katori and Ye alone is fair to other early lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) and to the proposers of the magic-wavelength condition.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a precondition or as a consequence.
Whether the credit for the first lattice-clock demonstrations should be described in the citation with respect to Ye's JILA clocks and the many-body clock work as a separate, distinct contribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B012. I have no tie to Katori or Ye. My own work is on rare-earth-doped crystals and slow-light laser stabilization, which is adjacent to frequency-stabilization but not a collaboration. I do lead part of WACQT, which is Chalmers-based and so overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home, and circuit QED (B005) is in his field and the centre's field; that candidate is not in my preferred configuration, and I would defer to him on it.
